claims.text: Rapid thermal processing limits atomic diffusion in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Limited atomic diffusion traps local elemental inhomogeneities.
Limited atomic diffusion traps metastable phase assemblages.
Reducing heating and cooling rates and adding intermediate dwells increases atomic mobility and redistribution.
The increased redistribution produced by moderated thermal profiles promotes a homogeneous single-phase solid solution.
Flash-synthesized high-entropy alloy nanoparticles typically exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
The controlled intervention is to reduce heating and cooling rates and insert intermediate-temperature dwell periods while keeping nominal composition and atmosphere fixed.
Rapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles can use peak temperatures near 2000 K, an inert argon atmosphere, and processing times from milliseconds to seconds.
The proposed processing regime applies to fixed compositions containing more than five noble metals, exemplified by Pt, Ir, Rh, Os, and Ru.
Atomic diffusion and rearrangement during dwell periods are the structural mediator between the thermal intervention and phase formation.
Moderated thermal profiles will improve elemental homogeneity relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Moderated thermal profiles will reduce secondary-phase formation relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Moderated thermal profiles will improve control of nanoparticle morphology relative to rapid heating and cooling.
EDS mapping can be used to assess elemental-distribution homogeneity.
Sharper single-phase XRD patterns will indicate reduced secondary-phase content.
At sufficiently long reaction times or under conditions causing bulk sintering or equilibrium thermodynamic control, kinetic trapping becomes less important.
Element-specific diffusion rates may cause deviations from the predicted homogenization.

Failure of the moderated protocol to produce a statistically significant improvement in phase purity, elemental homogeneity, and morphology relative to the rapid-processing control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says rapid cycling and limited mobility impede homogeneous single-phase formation, whereas cited evidence reports that rapid cooling suppresses secondary phases and that limited free-atom mobility can make random-alloy formation more likely as the number of atom types increases.
